newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan minister calls offshore futures "positive".
newsitem.headline: Taiwan minister calls offshore futures "positive".

text.p: Finance Minister Paul Chiu said on Tuesday that Taiwan regarded as "positive" the offshore Taiwan stock index futures being launched on January 9 by exchanges in Singapore and Chicago, but vowed to monitor their impact.

"We hold a positive view but we will monitor them for a period of time," Chiu said in response to reporters' questions about the contracts being launched by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and Singapore International Monetary Exchange.

Taiwan, playing for time to build its own local futures infrastructure, has stopped short of deeming the rivals hostile but has withheld technical cooperation and threatened to cut off access to stock price data crucial to their indexes.

Regulators said on Saturday Taiwan's futures exchange launch would have to be postponed to 1998 from an already delayed target date of October, citing legislative bickering that has held up passage of an enabling Futures Trading Law.
The Securities and Exchange Commission also announced a half-year grace period during which it would monitor the offshore rivals but not interfere with their operations.
Aside from the CME and SIMEX initiatives, San Francisco's Pacific Stock Exchange will launch trading Taiwan stock-index options on January 9.
Taiwan's stock exchange plans to offer index options but not likely before mid-1997, while the launch of Taiwan's own futures contracts must await establishment of a futures exchange.
Futures brokerages and investors have pressured regulators in the meantime to lift restrictions barring local trading of the offshore contracts, but the commission to date has baulked.
Investors are expected to skirt the ban by opening underground offshore accounts and trading by telephone.
Analysts say local investors, who can legally trade nearly 100 overseas commodities futures contracts, have legitimate need of a stock market hedge.
Experts estimate Taiwan stock-index futures could fuel T$50 billion (US$1.8 billion) a month in first-year turnover, a market the CME, SIMEX and Pacific exchange are eager to tap.

Taiwan regulators reserve a right to cut off real-time stock price data to Dow Jones and Co's Taiwan index, to be used by the Merc and Pacific exchange, and one compiled by a Morgan Stanley group unit that underlies the SIMEX contracts.
Dow Jones and Morgan Stanley say their Taiwan indexes have quite high correlations to the Taiwan exchange's TAIEX index, which has not been made available to the offshore competitors.
Despite the ban on local trading of offshore futures, Taiwan regulators have not acted to block real-time data about them.

Jurisdictional wrangling in Taiwan has stalled local launch of the GLOBEX system on which the CME's Taiwan futures will be traded. GLOBEX is a partnership of the CME, Reuters Holdings Plc and Marche a Terme International of France.
